evidence.title: Pulmonary pulsatility quantified by electrical impedance tomography in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome patients undergoing extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support.
evidence.abstract: Background The cardiac-related pulsatility signal from electrical impedance tomography (EIT) correlates with stroke volume in mechanically ventilated patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). However, in swine models, regional pulsatility amplitude was also shown to increase with downstream flow obstruction. We aimed to investigate the relationship between regional pulsatility and pulmonary hemodynamics in a cohort of severe ARDS patients on veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Methods We reanalysed data obtained from 20 ARDS patients receiving ECMO support. EIT was recorded 30 min after adjusting ECMO blood flow to target three ranges of mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO 2 ) (70-75 %; 75-80 %; >80%), applied in random order. Ventilation was protective with PEEP 15[12-16] cmH 2 O, Vt 4 ± 1 ml/kg PBW. Quality of EIT tracings allowed for separate modelling of pulsatility and ventilation in 16/20 patients. EIT units were calibrated to millilitres of tidal volume (ml*) using synchronised tidal volume measurements, allowing for between-patient comparisons. Mixed-effects modelling was employed to account for repeated measurements. Results Across blood flow steps, pulsatility amplitude was directly related to stroke volume (SV) (β = 0.28 (0.06 - 0.5) ml*/mL, p = 0.014) and systolic pulmonary artery pressure (PAPs) (β = 0.47 (0.14 - 0.81) ml*/mmHg, p = 0.008) and inversely related to mixed venous oxygen tension (PvO 2 ) (β = -0.41 (-0.79--0.03) ml*/mmHg, p = 0.039). Changes in pulsatility had an 80% concordance rate with changes in SV and 83% with PAPs. At each ECMO blood flow step, there was a decrease in ventral lung pulsatility during inspiration (p 2 ; ρ = 0.59, p = 0.017 at Intermediate SvO 2 ; ρ = 0.81, p 2 ). Conclusion n severe ARDS patients on ECMO, pulsatility amplitude reflects stroke volume changes induced by positive intrathoracic pressures and mixed venous saturation targets. evidence.title: Experience in treating thrombosis after adjustment of a PICC catheter.
evidence.abstract: Peripheral central catheter related deep vein thrombosis (PICC-DVT) has been proven to be a significant cause of unplanned extubation. We reported a case of 78-year-old patient, whose PICC was found kinked. After the adjustment, the blood flowed smoothly again. On the next day, catheter was found to be occluded and Color Doppler Flow Imaging (CDFI) shown that it occurred multiple deep vein thrombosis. Based on this case and current literature, CDFI could be considered within the first 1-2 weeks after PICC placement and during follow-up in high-risk patients, particularly given that thrombosis may occur early and may be clinically silent.

evidence.title: Conceptual Reconsideration of the Classification of Pulmonary Hypertension: From 5 Groups to 2 Groups.
evidence.abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a hemodynamic condition arising from heterogeneous, often overlapping triggers. Although the etiology-driven 5-group classification provides an essential framework for disease definition and research standardization, it is frequently challenged in real-world practice, where cardiopulmonary multimorbidity is common and often delays therapeutic decision making. Here, we propose a complementary, treatment-oriented binary framework that stratifies pulmonary hypertension by dominant structural mechanisms: pulmonary microvasculopathy versus pulmonary large-vessel stenosis. Although anatomically grounded, this distinction primarily reflects pathophysiological processes, hemodynamic behaviors, and therapeutic responsiveness. Rather than supplanting current classifications, it highlights lesion-level features directly relevant to therapeutic strategy. We outline pragmatic diagnostic pathways integrating anatomical imaging, hemodynamic confirmation, and systematic evaluation of cardiopulmonary comorbidities, emphasizing early identification of potentially revascularizable large-vessel disease, where surgical or endovascular intervention may yield substantial and durable clinical benefit. This pathophysiology-driven perspective aims to simplify frontline decision making, reduce diagnostic delay, and support treatment precision across diverse clinical settings.

evidence.title: Spontaneous rupture of the iliac vein presenting with hemorrhagic shock and extensive venous thrombosis.
evidence.abstract: We report the case of a 48-year-old woman admitted with acute right flank pain and circulatory collapse. The initial diagnosis was right iliac vein thrombosis and a large retroperitoneal hematoma. Emergency surgery at a local hospital evacuated the hematoma and repaired the right external iliac vein. Postoperatively, she developed severe right leg swelling and pain, and limb-threatening ischemia with extensive right lower limb deep vein thrombosis. After transfer to our center, she underwent inferior vena cava filter placement and emergency thrombectomy. Our initial experience in approaching patients with deep vein thrombosis, abdominal pain, and shock considers spontaneous iliac vein rupture for timely intervention.

evidence.title: Management of Recurrent Venous Thromboembolism on Anticoagulation.
evidence.abstract: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are the standard first treatment for patients with venous thromboembolism. Unfortunately, some patients develop recurrent thromboembolism despite adherence to anticoagulation. This remains a significant clinical challenge with no randomized data to guide therapy. This review summarizes the available evidence for the management of recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) and DOAC failure, and we propose our group consensus and management algorithm.

warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Background The cardiac-related pulsatility signal from electrical impedance tomography (EIT) correlates with stroke volume in mechanically ventilated patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). However, in swine models, regional pulsatility amplitude was also shown to increase with downstream flow obstruction. We aimed to investigate the relationship between regional pulsatility and pulmonary hemodynamics in a cohort of severe ARDS patients on veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Methods We reanalysed data obtained from 20 ARDS patients receiving ECMO support. EIT was recorded 30 min after adjusting ECMO blood flow to target three ranges of mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO 2 ) (70-75 %; 75-80 %; >80%), applied in random order. Ventilation was protective with PEEP 15[12-16] cmH 2 O, Vt 4 ± 1 ml/kg PBW. Quality of EIT tracings allowed for separate modelling of pulsatility and ventilation in 16/20 patients. EIT units were calibrated to millilitres of tidal volume (ml*) using synchronised tidal volume measurements, allowing for between-patient comparisons. Mixed-effects modelling was employed to account for repeated measurements. Results Across blood flow steps, pulsatility amplitude was directly related to stroke volume (SV) (β = 0.28 (0.06 - 0.5) ml*/mL, p = 0.014) and systolic pulmonary artery pressure (PAPs) (β = 0.47 (0.14 - 0.81) ml*/mmHg, p = 0.008) and inversely related to mixed venous oxygen tension (PvO 2 ) (β = -0.41 (-0.79--0.03) ml*/mmHg, p = 0.039). Changes in pulsatility had an 80% concordance rate with changes in SV and 83% with PAPs. At each ECMO blood flow step, there was a decrease in ventral lung pulsatility during inspiration (p 2 ; ρ = 0.59, p = 0.017 at Intermediate SvO 2 ; ρ = 0.81, p 2 ). Conclusion n severe ARDS patients on ECMO, pulsatility amplitude reflects stroke volume changes induced by positive intrathoracic pressures and mixed venous saturation targets. custody_records.raw_content: Peripheral central catheter related deep vein thrombosis (PICC-DVT) has been proven to be a significant cause of unplanned extubation. We reported a case of 78-year-old patient, whose PICC was found kinked. After the adjustment, the blood flowed smoothly again. On the next day, catheter was found to be occluded and Color Doppler Flow Imaging (CDFI) shown that it occurred multiple deep vein thrombosis. Based on this case and current literature, CDFI could be considered within the first 1-2 weeks after PICC placement and during follow-up in high-risk patients, particularly given that thrombosis may occur early and may be clinically silent.

custody_records.raw_content: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a hemodynamic condition arising from heterogeneous, often overlapping triggers. Although the etiology-driven 5-group classification provides an essential framework for disease definition and research standardization, it is frequently challenged in real-world practice, where cardiopulmonary multimorbidity is common and often delays therapeutic decision making. Here, we propose a complementary, treatment-oriented binary framework that stratifies pulmonary hypertension by dominant structural mechanisms: pulmonary microvasculopathy versus pulmonary large-vessel stenosis. Although anatomically grounded, this distinction primarily reflects pathophysiological processes, hemodynamic behaviors, and therapeutic responsiveness. Rather than supplanting current classifications, it highlights lesion-level features directly relevant to therapeutic strategy. We outline pragmatic diagnostic pathways integrating anatomical imaging, hemodynamic confirmation, and systematic evaluation of cardiopulmonary comorbidities, emphasizing early identification of potentially revascularizable large-vessel disease, where surgical or endovascular intervention may yield substantial and durable clinical benefit. This pathophysiology-driven perspective aims to simplify frontline decision making, reduce diagnostic delay, and support treatment precision across diverse clinical settings.

custody_records.raw_content: We report the case of a 48-year-old woman admitted with acute right flank pain and circulatory collapse. The initial diagnosis was right iliac vein thrombosis and a large retroperitoneal hematoma. Emergency surgery at a local hospital evacuated the hematoma and repaired the right external iliac vein. Postoperatively, she developed severe right leg swelling and pain, and limb-threatening ischemia with extensive right lower limb deep vein thrombosis. After transfer to our center, she underwent inferior vena cava filter placement and emergency thrombectomy. Our initial experience in approaching patients with deep vein thrombosis, abdominal pain, and shock considers spontaneous iliac vein rupture for timely intervention.

custody_records.raw_content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are the standard first treatment for patients with venous thromboembolism. Unfortunately, some patients develop recurrent thromboembolism despite adherence to anticoagulation. This remains a significant clinical challenge with no randomized data to guide therapy. This review summarizes the available evidence for the management of recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) and DOAC failure, and we propose our group consensus and management algorithm.
